title: The Great War of the Worlds Panic Myth
summary: Josh and Chuck examine the 1938 Mercury Theater on the Air radio adaptation of H. G. Wells's The War of the Worlds, its realistic faux-news format, and the enduring myth that it caused nationwide panic. They cover Wells's novel and its themes, Orson Welles and John Houseman's production choices, the broadcast itself (including the Grover's Mill, New Jersey news-bulletin sequence), the newspaper panic coverage, Hadley Cantril's flawed 1940 study, Brad Schwartz's archival research showing panic was isolated, and the 1948 Quito, Ecuador broadcast that did cause deadly riots. The episode ends with a listener mail segment from Tom in the UK.
topics: War of the Worlds panic myth

segments.title: Opening banter and introduction
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck banter about doing a welcome for new listeners, then introduce the episode's somber subject: the War of the Worlds broadcast panic.

segments.title: H. G. Wells's novel and its themes
segments.summary: The War of the Worlds was the first alien invasion story, serialized in magazines before being published as a book. Its scariness came from societal breakdown in Victorian England and its subtext about human cruelty toward animals.
topics: The War of the Worlds novel

segments.title: Orson Welles's 1938 radio adaptation and production
segments.summary: Orson Welles and the Mercury Theater on the Air adapted the novel for Halloween 1938 during the Great Depression and tense pre-war period, using a verite faux-documentary style. The cast and writer Howard Koch had doubts about the early script, and Houseman pushed changes, including removing time passing and adding realistic details. Wells had last-minute changes made, and there were no sponsors.

segments.title: The broadcast's opening and news-bulletin format
segments.summary: The show aired Sunday, October 30 at 8 p.m.; the hosts' transcript says October 8 for the air date as stated. It opened with an announcer and a fake musical program from the Meridian Room of the Hotel Park Plaza, and then broke in with news bulletins about an object landing in New Jersey.

segments.title: Reporter Carl Phillips scene from Grover's Mill
segments.summary: Hosts read excerpts of the script in which a reporter, Carl Phillips, describes Martian machines and a heat-ray attack at Grover's Mill, with a Professor Pearson and state police present. The announcer also describes spreading attacks in other places.

segments.title: Competing programs and listener channel surfing
segments.summary: Hosts discuss the Chase and Sanborn Hour with Edgar Bergen and Charlie McCarthy airing opposite the Mercury broadcast, and how listeners without pause or recording could channel surf during commercial breaks.

segments.title: Newspaper reaction and Hadley Cantril's study
segments.summary: Newspapers the next day ran sensational headlines and reported panic, suicides, and heart attacks. Wells publicly apologized. Princeton psychologist Hadley Cantril's later book claimed about six million listeners and six frightened, based on interviews with 135 people in New Jersey, selecting 100 who had been scared, and extrapolating nationally.

segments.title: Brad Schwartz's research and the debunking of the panic myth
segments.summary: Later research found actual ratings were much lower, around two percent of respondents listening, and Cantril's numbers were far off. Brad Schwartz examined letters in the University of Michigan archives and found panic was sporadic and mostly in New Jersey, with many listeners thrilled. Newsroom call volume and unverified wire reports helped create the myth. The Manhattan couple who fled by train is described.
topics: War of the Worlds myth debunked

segments.title: The 1948 Quito, Ecuador broadcast riot
segments.summary: Eight years after the Mercury broadcast, a Quito, Ecuador radio station recreated the drama with other stations joining in. Listeners panicked, then grew angry on learning it was fiction, and a mob burned the newspaper building housing the station, killing six people and injuring fifteen. Two broadcasters were indicted.

segments.title: Wrap-up of the panic myth
segments.summary: The hosts summarize that the idea of widespread American panic is largely myth, with the exception of Ecuador.

segments.title: Listener mail from Tom in the UK
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck read a listener email from Tom, an engineer in Stoke-on-Trent, who praises the show and mentions Polish mayo and other emails he has sent.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts invite listeners to write in by email and close the episode with the show credits.
